abstract: Versatile Disk Video (DVD-Video) is a revolutionary new consumer video system. The expected demand for DVD programming represents a huge opportunity for the studios and content producers to profit from the sale of movies rereleased in this new format. Due to the richness and complexity of features and the image and sound quality of the format, content producers will need to work closely with DVD authoring facilities in the mastering of their movies to this new high-quality medium. From the facility's perspective, there are many steps involved in the DVD-Video authoring process. This paper will focus on the critical steps of element preparation, telecine transfer, video preprocessing, and compression that greatly influence the quality of the DVD-Video product.

authors.bio: C. Bradley Hunt is senior vice-president for DVD and Imaging Technologies at All Post, Inc., an audio and video post-production house in Burbank, Calif. He is responsible for managing the engineering, technology, and capital equipment decisions for the company. This has included the startup of All Post's new compression and DVD premastering facility. Prior to joining All Post, he was the director of operations for Eastman Kodak's Digital Motion Imaging Division. In this role, he was responsible for the manufacturing, worldwide customer service and support, and the international sales of Kodak's Cineon Digital Film System products. He also managed the Kodak/Philips BTS Spirit Datacine project. Prior to this, he lived in London on an expatriate assignment as Kodak's European sales manager for digital motion imaging products. Mr. Hunt was responsible for creating the strategic and business plans which led to Kodak's investment and startup of their Digital Motion Imaging line-of-business. He has held various positions in his 20-year career at Kodak including research and development, product planning, marketing, and field sales related to the motion picture and television industry. Hunt graduated from Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology with a Bachelor's degree in chemical engineering in 1976. He also received an M.B.A. degree, in 1990, from the William E. Simon Graduate School of Business Administration at the University of Rochester. He is an executive member of the Technology Council of the Motion Picture-Television Industry, a Fellow of SMPTE, and a two-time recipient of the SMPTE Journal Award.
